name: Bioconservatism
summary: Bioconservatism urges caution and restraint toward biotechnologies, especially human genetic modification, enhancement and radical life extension. Its adherents hold that human nature, with its limits, vulnerability and mortality, grounds human dignity and flourishing, and that democratic institutions should steer technology rather than let markets or science set the ends.
scope: The profile represents the bioethical current around Leon Kass and the US President's Council on Bioethics, Francis Fukuyama (Our Posthuman Future), Michael Sandel and Jurgen Habermas, as summarised in the Wikipedia article and the SEP entry on enhancement. Because these thinkers range from conservative to social-democratic, positions on general economic, social and foreign-policy questions are mostly left neutral and low confidence; only biotechnology, human nature, dignity and democratic control are stated positions.

keyFigures.name: Leon Kass
keyFigures.role: Bioethicist and chair of the US President's Council on Bioethics, author of Beyond Therapy.

keyFigures.name: Francis Fukuyama
keyFigures.role: Political theorist who argued in Our Posthuman Future that biotechnology threatens human nature and needs democratic regulation.

keyFigures.name: Michael Sandel
keyFigures.role: Philosopher who argues that enhancement erodes humility and the giftedness of life.

sources.usedFor: Scholarly summary of Kass, Sandel, Fukuyama, Habermas and Annas on enhancement and equality.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Bioconservative writers focus on enhancement, not health financing; Habermas and Sandel lean toward public provision while Kass and Fukuyama are mixed, so no common line is documented.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage policy is outside the bioconservative literature, and its leading figures span centre-left to neoconservative, so adherents are split.

public-ownership.rationale: Nothing in the bioconservative sources concerns ownership of utilities; the camp is divided between social democrats and conservatives on this.

property-fundamental.rationale: The literature is silent on property rights; Fukuyama and Kass lean conservative but Habermas and Sandel do not.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Not a bioconservative topic; the camp mixes civil-libertarian and security-minded thinkers.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Kass objects to shortcuts to happiness and mood-altering drugs that bypass effort, so adherents lean against recreational drug use, though legal policy is not set out.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Speech regulation falls outside the bioconservative literature and adherents are split.

state-harmful.rationale: Bioconservatism relies on the state and democratic institutions to regulate biotechnology, so the claim that the state is unnecessary and harmful is rejected.

limit-guns.rationale: Gun policy is unrelated to the bioconservative literature; adherents differ.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal policy is not covered by the sources and adherents are split.

traditional-family.rationale: Kass defends natural procreation and the generational family against technological reproduction, which supports the family's central role, but he and others do not endorse a single family model.

abortion-legal.rationale: Fukuyama gives embryos higher moral status than ordinary cells yet is not an absolutist, and Habermas and Sandel differ; adherents are split.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Not a bioconservative concern; the camp spans left and right.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Fukuyama defends species-typical human nature as rooted in biology and rejects pure social construction, so adherents lean to disagree, though the topic is not central.

gradual-change.rationale: Kass and Fukuyama counsel caution toward rapid technological change and respect for inherited human limits, which supports gradualism on the matters they discuss.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Fukuyama and Annas want international regulation of biotech, but wider empowerment of the UN is not a bioconservative claim, so adherents split.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Foreign policy is outside the literature and adherents differ.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Bioconservatism is defined by caution toward technologies that can compromise human dignity, chiefly biotechnology and enhancement; it is not opposed to technology in general.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Fukuyama favours state institutions sorting beneficial from harmful biotech, but directing investment generally is not a bioconservative claim.

democracy-best.rationale: Fukuyama says legitimate uses of science should be decided democratically by elected, informed representatives and Habermas ties his case to democratic moral equality; the 'even when voters choose badly' clause tempers this.

direct-votes.rationale: Fukuyama favours decisions through elected, scientifically informed representatives rather than direct votes, so adherents lean to disagree.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Kass and Sandel stress obligation, gratitude and community while Habermas stresses rights, so adherents are split.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Bioconservatives defend the natural as a moral category, including human nature shaped by evolution, which supports valuing nature in itself, although they speak mostly of human nature. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Bioconservatism urges caution and restraint toward biotechnologies and opposes transhumanism and the singularity, so speeding technological change despite disruption is rejected.

human-enhancement.rationale: Kass argues that enhancement bypasses effort, erodes human nature and makes achievements not fully our own, and bioconservatives broadly oppose it beyond therapy.

restore-past-order.rationale: Kass is conservative about human nature but does not call for restoring a lost social order; the camp is mixed.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Bioconservatives accept medicine and technology used for healing and defend civilisation's human goods, so abandoning it for foraging is not part of their view.

harm-principle.rationale: Bioconservatives hold that some uses of biotechnology, such as enhancement or cloning, should be limited even where no clear harm to others is shown, because of dignity and human nature, so a pure harm principle is rejected.

total-state.rationale: Bioconservatives want democratic regulation of a specific domain, not state direction of all life; Habermas and Fukuyama defend liberal democracy.

universal-morality.rationale: Fukuyama and Kass seek a positive account of human nature and dignity that holds for all humans, and Habermas defends universal moral equality, so adherents lean to agree.

single-common-good.rationale: Adherents want shared deliberation on the human good, but they accept pluralism in democracy, so they are split on one rational common good.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Habermas and Fukuyama argue secularly while Kass's humane reasoning cites reverence and gratitude, so adherents do not share a single stance.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Fukuyama's Factor X and Habermas's moral equality hold that all humans share dignity, so racial segregation is incompatible with the view. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Bioconservatives oppose genetic engineering of people and cite the eugenic past; Fukuyama and Habermas oppose state selection of human traits, so state discouragement of births by genetic status is rejected.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Bioconservatives require state regulation of biotechnology, which exceeds the night-watchman remit.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Fukuyama's shared-endowment account of human dignity and Habermas's moral equality contradict racial hierarchies. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Fukuyama's Factor X holds that all humans share an equal dignity rooted in a common endowment and Habermas treats genetic enhancement as a threat to moral equality, so equal worth is central.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Fukuyama holds that legitimate science policy must be decided by the democratic community acting through elected representatives, which supports the principle of consent.

population-transfer.rationale: Dignity of every human person is central, so forcing a minority to leave is incompatible with the view. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Kass warns that competitive pressure pushes people toward enhancement they would not otherwise choose, so adherents resist treating struggle as the main engine of progress.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Habermas's worry about asymmetrical parent-child domination is related, but adherents have no shared view on republican freedom; no direct statement.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Fukuyama and Kass ground their account of human nature in evolutionary biology, so adherents do not favour teaching creationism in public schools.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Kass is conservative on the degradation of sexuality but Habermas and Sandel are liberal; no common position.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Bioconservatism urges caution and restraint toward novel biotechnologies even before outcomes are known, which is a precautionary stance, though the statement concerns environmental risks specifically. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Their case rests on the equal dignity of all humans and democratic legitimacy, which excludes a sacred ruler. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

character-from-environment.rationale: Fukuyama defines human nature as species-typical traits that come from genetics, not just environment, and Kass defends innate nature, so adherents lean against character being formed mainly by circumstance.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Fukuyama and Habermas place political authority within law and democratic accountability.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Habermas's equality argument leans toward abolition but Kass and Fukuyama are silent on titles, so adherents are unsettled.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Fukuyama's shared-dignity universalism does not support ranking societies by advancement, though empire is never discussed.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Admissions policy is outside the literature; adherents split along their wider politics.

public-money-creation.rationale: Monetary policy never appears in the bioconservative sources.

delink-world-market.rationale: Development strategy never appears in these sources.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Kass worries about drugs and media making people content without effort, but the claim about social reproduction is Marxist and not shared.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Habermas leans to yes and Fukuyama is mixed; the literature does not discuss constitutional founding values.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Fukuyama accepts cross-country variation in ethical views and political systems but still wants harmonised biotech rules; no clear stance on this claim.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Kass defends natural procreation and generational renewal but sets out no incentive policy.

defeat-communism.rationale: Fukuyama is associated with the Cold War liberal outlook but the sources here do not take this up.

religion-illusion.rationale: Kass, whose reasoning draws on reverence and gratitude toward life, would not call religion an illusion; Habermas is a secular but respectful, so mild disagreement.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language policy is not a bioconservative subject.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Bioconservatives cite eugenics and the Nazi past as warnings, and nothing in their sources questions the Holocaust; Habermas and Fukuyama are mainstream historians-aware scholars. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Democratic deliberation is their prescribed route to governing biotech, so suppressing opposition is rejected.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Habermas and Sandel favour public deliberation, but Fukuyama prefers informed representatives; split.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Kass is conservative on bodily nature while Habermas and Sandel are liberal; no shared position.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Habermas and Fukuyama argue secularly and Fukuyama locates legitimacy in the democratic community, so divine authority is not the shared position.

property-franchise.rationale: Equal moral standing is central to Habermas and Fukuyama, which excludes a wealth-based franchise. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

racial-franchise.rationale: Equal dignity of all humans is central, ruling out limiting the franchise by race. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Equal dignity of all humans means targeting a religious minority is rejected. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Kass's account of gratitude toward the given and reverence for life and Habermas's respect for religious sources both oppose coercive atheism.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Bioconservatives share a worry about catastrophic technological outcomes, such as Fukuyama's comparison with nuclear weapons, but existential-risk language is more associated with their transhumanist opponents.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Kass values earned achievement over unearned results, which hints at agreement for work, but he does not address property income.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Fukuyama defines human nature as species-typical, biologically grounded traits and Kass defends natural embodiment and sexual procreation, so adherents reject that sex is a social construction.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its rationale rests on dramatically expanded funding, radical life extension or animal experiments, and the statement now asks only whether governments should fund research aimed at slowing biological ageing.

reviewHistory.rationale: Kass argues against radical life extension, saying finitude and generational succession are essential to human goods, so dramatically expanded funding to defeat ageing is rejected; modest therapeutic research on age-related disease is another matter.

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its rationale rests on dramatically expanded funding, radical life extension or animal experiments, and the statement now asks only whether governments should fund research aimed at slowing biological ageing.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

spiritual-nature.rationale: Kass appeals to a positive account of human nature and dignity that goes beyond the material and draws on reverence, and Fukuyama's Factor X includes moral choice and consciousness, so adherents lean to agree.

future-generations.rationale: Kass worries that changing human nature through biotechnology affects future generations and Fukuyama's concern is the posthuman future, so adherents lean to agree that heritage should be handed on intact, even though the statement is about the Earth. None of the cited sources takes up this statement, so this is a low-confidence reading of the general outlook.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Bioconservatism relies on strong democratic state institutions to regulate biotechnology, so smashing the state is rejected.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Fukuyama's Factor X and Kass's positive account of human nature are central to the position.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Student debt is outside bioconservatism, and its thinkers range from conservative to social-democratic.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Bioconservatism does not address the unity of religions; Kass appeals to religious tradition but the thinkers include secular figures like Habermas, so adherents split.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Pollution policy is outside the literature; Fukuyama favours democratic state control of technology but nothing is stated on tort liability.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Bioconservatives urge restraint on technology for human nature, but their stated concern is human nature and not ecology, and the sources give no common position.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Criminal sentencing is outside the bioconservative literature, and its figures differ along ordinary political lines.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Immigration and language are outside the bioconservative literature, and its figures differ along ordinary political lines.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Bioethical writers do not address state recognition of religious interpretations; Kass draws on religious tradition while Habermas and Sandel are secular.

premarital-sex.rationale: Sexual morality is not part of the core bioconservative case; Kass is traditional while Sandel and Habermas are liberal.

race-social-construct.rationale: Fukuyama defends a universal human nature and equal dignity, but the literature does not address the scientific status of racial categories.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: The thinkers stress human dignity and legal limits on technology; none address drug policy, but extrajudicial killing contradicts the dignity they defend.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Bioconservatives hold that technology should be constrained by human nature and dignity rather than combined freely with progress, though the ancestral-values wording is not theirs.

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: Not a bioconservative topic. (Carried over from former-empire-influence, "A country should cultivate political and cultural influence in regions once ruled by its predecessor empire.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: Parents should not be allowed to select or modify the genetic traits of their children beyond preventing disease.
missingStatements.rationale: Habermas, Sandel and Kass each oppose prenatal trait design as undermining the child's freedom and the parent-child relation, and the SEP entry gives this as a core bioconservative claim.

missingStatements.text: Aging and death are part of a good human life and should not be abolished.
missingStatements.rationale: Kass argues that finitude is the source of aspiration, love and virtue and opposes radical life extension.

missingStatements.text: Human genetic modification that can be passed to later generations should be prohibited by law.
missingStatements.rationale: Fukuyama argues for state control of biotechnology and Annas proposes a species-protection treaty to stop germline change that threatens human nature.

missingStatements.text: There is a shared human nature that grounds human dignity and rights and should not be redesigned.
missingStatements.rationale: Fukuyama's Factor X and Kass's positive account of human nature are central to the position.

notes: Adherents are politically heterogeneous (Kass and Fukuyama conservative or neoconservative, Sandel communitarian, Habermas social-democratic), so most answers outside bioethics are neutral or inferred. Many 0 answers reflect that split, not indifference.
